subject: mathematics_2b
question_text: Show that the area of the region bounded by the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 is πab. Hence deduce the area of the circle x² + y² = a².

mark_split.label: Solve for y and locate the x-intercept
Integrate over the first quadrant to get πab
Deduce the area of the circle

steps.label: Solve for y and locate the x-intercept
steps.margin_note: First mark. y = (b/a)√(a²−x²) — the ellipse's y-value is a circle of radius a's y-value, multiplied by the factor b/a.
steps.memory_tip: Setting y=0 in the ellipse equation always gives x=±a, the ends of the horizontal (major) axis.
lines: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 ⇒ y²/b² = 1 − x²/a² ⇒ y² = b²[(a² − x²)/a²] ⇒ y = (b/a)√(a² − x²)
Put y = 0 ⇒ √(a² − x²) = 0 ⇒ x² = a² ⇒ x = a
steps.why: Solving the ellipse equation for y gives the upper half of the curve as a function of x, and setting y=0 finds where the curve meets the x-axis — at x=a, the semi-major-axis length.
common_mistakes: Losing the factor b/a when solving for y, and writing y=√(a²−x²), which is the equation of a circle of radius a, not the ellipse.
Taking the x-intercept as x=b instead of x=a.

steps.label: See the first-quadrant region OAB
steps.margin_note: The ellipse is symmetric about both axes, so the whole area is 4 times the shaded first-quadrant piece OAB.
steps.memory_tip: Any curve symmetric about both axes has its total enclosed area equal to 4 times its first-quadrant area.
steps.why: By the symmetry of the ellipse about both axes, the full enclosed area is exactly four times the area of the region in the first quadrant bounded by the curve, the x-axis and the y-axis — the picture makes this quartering visible.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the factor of 4 and reporting the first-quadrant area alone as the total area of the ellipse.
Shading the wrong quadrant or a region that does not match the labelled points O, A, B.

steps.label: Integrate over the first quadrant to get πab
steps.margin_note: Two marks. (4b/a)(a²/2)(π/2) simplifies step by step: 4/a×a²=4a, then 4a×b/2=2ab, then 2ab×π/2=πab.
steps.memory_tip: The final simplification always collapses to πab regardless of a and b individually — a clean, symmetric result.
lines: Required area = 4 (area of OAB) = 4∫₀^a y dx = 4∫₀^a (b/a)√(a² − x²) dx

lines.text: ∴ Area of the ellipse = πab sq. units

steps.why: Applying the standard ∫√(a²−x²)dx formula, the algebraic term vanishes at both x=0 (where it's already 0) and x=a (where √(a²−x²)=0), leaving only the inverse-sine term; substituting Sin⁻¹(1)=π/2 and simplifying (4b/a)(a²/2)(π/2) collapses neatly to πab.
common_mistakes: Losing track of the b/a and a²/2 factors while combining them into the final πab.
Using Sin⁻¹(1)=π instead of the correct π/2.

steps.label: Deduce the area of the circle
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Substituting b=a into πab is the whole deduction — no fresh integration is needed.
steps.memory_tip: A circle is an ellipse with equal axes — setting b=a in any ellipse formula gives the matching circle formula.
lines: If b = a, the ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 becomes x²/a² + y²/a² = 1, i.e. x² + y² = a²
Putting b = a in the area formula πab gives

lines.text: ∴ Area of the circle x² + y² = a² is πa² sq. units

steps.why: A circle is the special case of an ellipse where both semi-axes are equal (b=a); substituting b=a directly into the just-proved formula πab gives πa·a=πa², the familiar area of a circle of radius a.
common_mistakes: Re-deriving the circle's area from scratch instead of simply substituting b=a into the ellipse formula already proved.
Writing the final circle area as πa instead of πa².
